_README.what: Per-crag facts extracted from .claude/docs/rock-drying-research.md and .claude/docs/climbing-terminology-research.md. Phase 2 of docs/handoffs/climbing-research-brief-v1.md.
_README.status: RESEARCH DATA, NOT A SCHEMA. Nothing reads this file. It does not imply a migration and no field here maps to a column.
_README.null_rule: null means UNKNOWN and must never render as a favourable value. A crag with no seepage information has seepage_prone: null, never false. See .claude/rules/defect-patterns.md §1.
_README.field_shape: Every non-identity field is either null, or an object { value, source, confidence }. There is no bare value anywhere: a fact without a source is not a fact. 'source' cites the section the claim was extracted from; follow it there for the underlying citation.

confidence.M: Measured — peer-reviewed rock-mechanics or petrophysics literature
confidence.C: Climbing-community convention, guidebook, or land-manager guidance
confidence.I: Inference in the source document, not stated by any cited source
confidence.X: The cited source was opened and does not support the claim (added 2026-09-16)

_README.seepage_rule: §4.16 corrected the tufa rule to SUFFICIENT, NOT NECESSARY. water_features true implies water has run over that face (high confidence). water_features false implies NOTHING about dryness — conduit and catchment seepage leaves no trace. Therefore seepage_prone is null wherever the only evidence is absence of tufa. A 'no' here must never read as reassurance.

seepage_mechanism.face_flow: Water moving over the exposed face with residence time. Leaves tufa, eyebrows, solution pockets. Observable from a guidebook photo.
seepage_mechanism.conduit: Water routed through joints, bedding planes, or from a body above (snowfield, river, ski area, loess cap). Leaves nothing on the face. Local knowledge only, per §2.3.

_README.not_in_the_brief_schema: Five fields were added because the research kept producing facts the proposed shape could not hold: season_gate, access_rules, unmodelled_input, seepage_mechanism, and aka. §4.13 lists five limiters the app does not model and four of them had nowhere to go. 'state' became 'region' + 'country' because a third of these crags are not in the US.

rock.note: Cherty, bedded, crimpy — the climbing is on the dolomite cap, with Jordan Sandstone below the routes. Commonly mislabelled sandstone. Two-material rock: dolomite (Mohs 3.5-4) studded with chert (Mohs 7, ~zero porosity), and the interface is where holds loosen.

unmodelled_input.value: ~35 ft of glacial sand, gravel and loess capping the steep slopes above the cliff line acts as a catchment. The face surface-dries in hours; the crag can stay damp much longer, worst at spring thaw.

rock.note: Steep sport amphitheatre in the Willow Falls gorge.

closure.reason: Closed Saturdays, restricted Friday and Sunday

unmodelled_input.value: The best documented seepage case in the research. Community guidance names FOUR inputs: 'certain combinations of humidity, precipitation, snowmelt, and/or river levels can leave the cliff wet and unclimbable due to seep'. The app models one of the four. Snowmelt is unmodelled; river level has no data source.

rock.note: Dense columnar type, 0.1-1.0% porosity: hours, not days, and no integrity risk. Eroded into the St. Croix Dalles.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: faster than Red Wing — dense basalt against cherty dolomite

unmodelled_input.value: The potholes and the river-level base pond water independently of the rock.

rock.note: In a quarry. Quarried faces have no case hardening — no protective rind, which removes the thin-shell failure mode but also removes the armour. Hinckley was selected commercially as a structural building stone, a strong signal it sits near the well-lithified end. No porosity or absorption figures found for it.

unmodelled_input.value: The ice park is FARMED — four managed areas are deliberately watered all winter. Those walls take annual full saturation plus freeze-thaw by design, and in shoulder season can be soaking for reasons no forecast can see.

rock.note: Mid-spectrum Ozark sandstone.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: 24-48h after moderate rain, longer for prolonged storms; the humid Ozark summer suppresses the stage-1 evaporation rate that does most of the work

rock.formation: Midcontinent Rift rhyolite, 1096.6 Ma, capping softer basalt
rock.note: Dense fine-grained volcanic rock: low porosity, fast-drying, friction-limited. Not a family the RockType enum has.

access_rules.value: Strict no-chalk ethic; free state-park permit required

unmodelled_input.value: The real conditions inputs are Lake Superior spray and fog, not rainfall.

rock.formation: Anorthosite blocks that punched through the rift magma, surrounding melt becoming diabase
rock.note: Described as abrasive. Dense plutonic: drying-trivial, friction-led. Same family as Poke-O-Moonshine.
Pink escarpment on the prairie. Near-zero matrix porosity; fracture drainage only.

Grain size varies WITHIN the same batholith — fine-grained at Mount Rushmore, coarse with abundant pegmatite crystals at the Needles. Those crystals ARE the holds. Drying is trivial; the wet-failure vector is crystal detachment rather than surface spalling.

rock.formation: Pahasapa Limestone (Mississippian, equivalent to the Madison)
rock.note: 475-600 ft of capstone, ~600 routes over ~19 crags. Finely crystalline beds interspersed by chert lenses and solution breccias, giving the cavernous, pocketed character. Rock quality improves further up the canyon — a within-crag gradient. Chert-in-carbonate is a repeated pattern with Red Wing's Oneota, not a one-off.

season_gate.value: Spring through June can be wet, though usually partly climbable

rock.note: Coarse-grained and famously sharp: alkali feldspar crystals 1-2 cm across with 'scalpel-like edges'. Landscape shaped by differential weathering along ENE joints. Drying is granite-fast; the coarse texture means skin, not conditions, is the limiter. Coarse biotite-rich granite weathers to grus, and a grussy rind holds water over an impermeable core.
Pocketed dolomite at ~2,600 m. Pocketed dolomite holds standing water in pockets long after the face dries.

season_gate.value: Season begins when the snow melts (early June) and runs to late autumn. ALTITUDE GATES THE SEASON HERE, NOT RAINFALL — a conditions model that answers 'dry' in April is answering the wrong question.

unmodelled_input.value: Snowmelt

rock.note: BREAKS THE ONE-LOCATION-ONE-ROCK-TYPE MODEL OUTRIGHT: 'The rock type changes from sandstone to limestone to granite the higher you go.' One canyon, one lat/lon, three drying classes stacked vertically. The schema cannot express it and averaging them would be wrong in both directions.

Park guidance names a mechanism the model does not have: sandstone 'absorbs water like a sponge, and the rock SWELLS AND DECOMPRESSES AS IT DRIES. During this process, it is extremely fragile.' If right, the drying transient is its own hazard state rather than a monotonic improvement — which sits awkwardly against the score's smooth linear ramp. Land-manager guidance, NOT lab-verified.

access_rules.value: All chalk and substitutes banned; free annual permit mandatory

dries_fast_relative_to.value: A local guide service reschedules for at least 24h after significant precipitation, and 2-3 days after snow, cloud or persistent rain

rock.formation: Fish Canyon Tuff, La Garita Caldera ~28 Ma
rock.note: 'Bulletproof rock with great friction', textured by quartz and sanidine crystals, hueco-ridden walls. Confirms the welding spectrum: densely welded tuff behaves near-granitic, non-welded Bishop Tuff does not. Not a family the RockType enum has.

water_features.value: huecos — hold water independently of the rock

rock.note: 1,000+ sport routes. Trad is considered dangerous because the limestone is brittle — so 'dry' and 'safe' are not the same claim here.

aspect.value: THE ASPECT-PLANNING CRAG. ~250 sunny days, winter highs in the 40s-50s °F, and the explicit local strategy is ASPECT ROTATION: climb the sun-facing walls in winter and the shaded ones in summer. The unimplemented aspect/solar term is not a refinement here — it IS the product.

rock.formation: Migmatitic biotite gneiss and gneissic granite
rock.note: Locally 'sandy granite', distinct from Boulder Canyon's granite sweeps. Metamorphic drainage behaviour: low matrix porosity, water tracking along foliation and folds.

Coarse feldspar-rich conglomeratic sandstone. Guide-service framing: 'harder and less fragile than many desert sandstones, but wet stone is slick, FLAKES CAN SEEP'. A sandstone whose limiter is friction and seepage, not structure.

crags.name: Rifle Mountain Park

rock.note: 'Varies both in quality and aspect from wall to wall.' The Wasteland has 'pocket and tufa-riddled stone'; the Arsenal has 'miniature tufas'.

water_features.value: tufas and pockets, concentrated in the Wasteland and the Arsenal

season_gate.value: SECTOR-LEVEL, MONTH-SCALE: 'Oftentimes the Wasteland and the left side of the Project Wall do not dry out until June.' Spring runoff is the driver, and the same seepage farms the canyon's winter ice. No rock-type constant can produce a per-sector June date.

unmodelled_input.value: Spring runoff

crags._why_this_crag_matters: THE WITHIN-CRAG CONTROL for the tufa rule. Same canyon, same limestone, same spring runoff — and the tufa-riddled sector is the named wet one. Worth more than the seven between-crag cases in §4.15 combined, because everything except the rock face is held constant.

rock.note: Bomber.

aspect.value: The feature climbers name first is a 'friendly southerly aspect'

rock.formation: Aztec Sandstone — the same Jurassic dune system as Zion's Navajo
rock.note: Eolian, weak calcium-carbonate cement, friable and very porous. The 'do not climb wet' class. Measured facies within the Navajo span ~28% porosity / 100 mD (dune) to 10% / 0.265 mD (wavy algal-matted) — a ~400x permeability spread inside one formation, the kind of difference you can walk past between two sectors of one canyon.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: BLM land-manager guidance is 24-48h after major rain or snow; community guidance increasingly says that is too short — 36 hours minimum, up to 3 days after heavy prolonged storms, and 5 days to a week after the biggest. The conditional version is the useful one: ~24h needs air above ~70°F, a southerly sunny aspect, and only a couple of hours of rain; cold, shady or big-storm cases want 48-72h.

rock.note: The high-altitude summer counterpart to Red Rock.

season_gate.value: Altitude makes it the summer option when Red Rock is too hot

rock.note: Same Jurassic dune system as Red Rock's Aztec. Weak calcium-carbonate cement, friable and very porous.

rock.formation: Wingate Sandstone (Late Triassic eolian), with Cedar Mesa Sandstone below
rock.note: The homogeneous composition and cementation is exactly what produces the splitter joint systems, and the cementing agents binding the quartz grains — CALCITE AND CLAY — are hydro-sensitive. The 24-to-48-hour rule exists here for that reason.

THE CLIMBING SURFACE IS NOT THE ROCK. The towers are draped in mud curtains; the rock is 'actually very hard' but what you climb is a thick mud layer — mud chimneys, bolts protruding inches from erosion, fixed slings drilled through rock. A drying model keyed to rock type is meaningless here: dried mud rehydrates on a completely different curve from the sandstone under it. The most extreme 'rock type is the wrong variable' case in the research.
Described as slippery and hard. Adjacent to Little Cottonwood and NOT interchangeable with it.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Dries fast; friction-limited

rock.note: Adjacent canyon to Big Cottonwood, different rock. Both dry fast, both friction-limited, not interchangeable.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Dries fast; friction-limited

rock.note: Rounded cobbles — frequently quartzite, so near-zero porosity — set in a sandy or calcareous MATRIX that is far more porous. The cobbles are dry almost immediately; the matrix holding them in is not. The wet failure mode is a cobble pulling out of a softened matrix, so THE DRYING TIME IS THE MATRIX'S, AND IT IS INVISIBLE FROM THE SURFACE. Needs its own class, keyed to matrix type, and it should be conservative.

Up to 98% QUARTZ, with case hardening and limonite cement veins along tectonic joints. A WVU thesis identified a 15-20 m homogeneous quartz-arenite interval lacking bedding-plane partings as the desirable climbing horizon; the basal conglomerate and underlying shale are weaker. THE DRYING CLASS CHANGES WITH HEIGHT ON THE SAME CLIFF. Silica-cemented quartz arenite: climbs wet, essentially undamaged.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Far faster than the eolian sandstones — ~0% measured strength loss when wet for this sub-class

unmodelled_input.value: Vertical variation within one cliff — the Nuttall result. The app has one rock type per location and a route-level property would be a much larger change.

rock.note: Quartz conglomerate whose cement is dominantly silica with relatively little iron oxide, described as one of the hardest and most durable of rocks. BEHAVES FAR CLOSER TO QUARTZITE THAN TO SANDSTONE.
Microcrystalline quartz coatings on the grains inhibit further quartz cement growth and PRESERVE ANOMALOUSLY HIGH POROSITY — simultaneously silica-cemented and porous.

access_rules.value: Explicit no-wet-climbing ethic. A GOOD CEMENT DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY LICENSE CLIMBING WET — here it is the sculpted surface patina that breaks, not the rock.

crags.name: Red River Gorge

rock.formation: Corbin Sandstone Member, Early Pennsylvanian, 30-85 m thick
rock.note: Quartz arenite ranging fine-grained to conglomeratic, iron-rich and orange-red in places. Sits between classes: solid overall, but FRIABLE IN CERTAIN AREAS, PARTICULARLY AFTER RAINFALL.

shelter.value: THE STANDING EXAMPLE OF GEOMETRY BEATING ROCK TYPE — its overhangs stay dry through rain that shuts everything else down. At sector grain: Bob Marley cave is 'surely one of the driest locations in the Red,' with a breeze that keeps condensation away 'when other crags are beaded with water'. Condensation is crag-specific within one gorge on one day, so it cannot be derived from a grid-cell forecast.

crags._why_this_crag_matters: Guidebooks for the Red carry PER-CRAG ICONS FOR SUN EXPOSURE AND RAIN PROTECTION alongside driving and walking times. The seepage_prone / rain-shelter flag proposed in §7 is not a novel schema invention — guidebook publishers already ship that field.

crags.name: Stanage and the Peak District grit

rock.note: Coarse quartz-feldspathic sandstone from delta deposits. Feldspar at Mohs 6 weathers to clay in a way quartz does not, which is the mechanistic reason grit sits below the arenites. Reported ~41% weaker when wet — a climbing-media figure whose primary source could NOT be reached (climbing.com is behind a login wall). Treat as indicative.
~1,100 towers of mostly highly weathered, EXTREMELY SOFT sandstone. Weakly cemented / structurally marginal.

access_rules.value: Climbing is PROHIBITED on rainy days and the following day — a rule, not advice. Note the implied drying model: a flat 24h from the END OF RAIN, regardless of amount.

rock.note: So soft that lead climbing is banned outright. THE ROCK HAS ONLY A THIN OUTER LAYER and that rind is the entire load-bearing structure — the extreme end of case hardening: protective while intact, catastrophic once wet.

access_rules.value: Lead climbing banned; everything top-roped on static rope

rock.note: The rock generally DRIES FAST, but if the winter has been rainy the TUFAS may be seeping, and dripping stalactites in spring are softer and more likely to break. So the same crag on the same day has a fast-drying vertical wall and a soft, seeping, breakable tufa line. FEATURE TYPE BEATS ROCK TYPE.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: The face dries fast; the tufa lines do not

rock.note: DOLOMITE, NOT LIMESTONE, though the climbing is hard to distinguish. Massive, cliff-forming, mildly overhung, defined by POCKETS (monos to jugs) with a surface soft enough that 'comfortizing' edges is a local norm. Pockets hold standing water; Red Wing's crimps and edges shed it — reasoning about one from the other gets the drying behaviour backwards.

water_features.value: pockets — hold standing water long after the face dries

rock.note: Dense micritic limestone — low porosity, dries fast at the surface, seeps for days.

approach_hazard.value: Cornice danger early in the season after a heavy-snow winter

season_gate.value: ~2,100 m; season late spring to autumn

unmodelled_input.value: THE CATCHMENT ARGUMENT MADE LITERAL: the area above the crag is a SKI AREA, and seepage follows a heavy-snow winter. The thing draining onto the wall is a snowfield.

rock.note: Dense micritic limestone — low porosity, dries fast at the surface, seeps for days.

Fresh, fine-grained plutonic rock — near-zero effective porosity, surface-film drying only. The safest family to climb wet: strong, barely porous, dries quickly; the practical cost is that shoe rubber does not stick.

water_features.value: Weathering pits and dishes on low-angle granite hold standing water for days after the wall itself is dry. Slabs are the one granite case where drying time is not trivial.

season_gate.value: THE LIMITER IS A ROAD. Season runs roughly June to October because Tioga Pass (Highway 120) closes on the first snow, usually November, and reopens late May to June depending on the snow year. The rock can be bone dry and the answer still 'no'. Unlike a ski field above the crag or snowmelt, it does not even correlate with conditions at the crag once the road is open.

unmodelled_input.value: Road and pass status — an access-infrastructure limiter class of its own

rock.note: Coarse, biotite-rich, weathered granite. Biotite expands by absorbing water, freeing crystals and disaggregating the rock into GRUS; darker biotite-rich and coarser-grained granites weather to grus much more readily than light, fine-grained ones. A grussy weathered rind holds water like a sponge over an impermeable core — THE WEATHERED SURFACE, NOT THE GRANITE, SETS THE DRYING TIME.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: SLOWER than fine-grained granite, despite the same family — the grus rind is the variable

rock.note: ~1% porosity. Coarse, biotite-rich, weathered granite — grus-prone per §4.3. Fifteen minutes' drive from Bishop Tuff at 38-60% porosity: one town spanning most of the porosity range in the whole reference table.

rock.formation: Welded rhyolite ash/tuff, ~30 Ma, Crooked River caldera
rock.note: Welded tuffs become hard rock because of heat and compaction during emplacement, and Smith's is popular precisely because it DOES NOT CRUMBLE EASILY. Behaves close to granite. The RockType enum has no tuff at all — §6.1's tuff half is still open and Smith has no correct label.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Near-granitic

rock.note: 38-60% POROSITY at densities of 1.1-1.5 g/cm³, most samples 45-57%. THAT IS MORE POROUS THAN ANY SANDSTONE IN THE RESEARCH. Welding varies laterally and vertically within the sheet, and localisation of fracturing tracks the degree of welding. No correct label in the RockType enum.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: SLOWER than any sandstone in the table, on porosity alone

rock.note: Same unit as the Happy and Sad Boulders, cut by the Owens River. Welding varies within the sheet so the local degree of welding is unrecorded here. No correct label in the RockType enum.
Dense columnar basalt, near-impermeable at 0.1-1.0% porosity.

rock.formation: Columnar-jointed porphyritic phonolite porphyry, Eocene ~49 Ma
rock.note: DEVILS TOWER IS NOT BASALT — the label is simply wrong in most sources. Drying-wise it behaves like dense plutonic rock.

closure.reason: Voluntary climbing closure for Native American cultural observance
closure.source: rock-drying-research.md §13 (terminology doc) — NOT independently verified here

rock.note: Very similar to the Gunks rock, highly erosion-resistant. Effectively zero matrix porosity; all water lives in fractures and drains by gravity.

Schist with some granite, and its FOLIATION — the tendency to fracture along parallel layers — is what makes the holds. Matrix porosity is low, but those same foliation planes are drainage paths, so water tracks along and emerges from them long after the face looks dry.
Low matrix porosity, fracture- and foliation-controlled permeability.
Low matrix porosity, fracture- and foliation-controlled permeability.

Cobbles dry almost immediately; the matrix holding them in does not. The wet failure mode is a cobble pulling out of a softened matrix, and the drying time is the matrix's — invisible from the surface.
Matrix-controlled drying per §4.6.
Matrix-controlled drying per §4.6.
Matrix-controlled drying per §4.6.

THE CLEANEST NATURAL EXPERIMENT AVAILABLE, paired with the Grampians. Same original sediment; a volcanic incursion ~400 Ma contact-metamorphosed the Arapiles rock to quartzite while the Grampians stayed sandstone. Adjacent areas, one protolith, OPPOSITE WET-WEATHER RULES. Nothing about the sediment predicted it; the thermal history did.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Much faster than the adjacent Grampians, on identical original sediment

rock.note: 'Often of a softer variety'. The unmetamorphosed half of the Arapiles natural experiment.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Much slower than adjacent Arapiles

rock.note: THE FAST-DRYING CHAMPION, and the community states the mechanism itself: 'the layering of minerals means that water can't easily penetrate... slate doesn't have pore spaces like sandstone does. So in the absence of crack systems slate dries quickly.' Note the qualifier — fracture drainage is the exception. The limiter is friction: slate slabs are notoriously frictionless with no protruding crystals.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: The fastest-drying rock in the document

rock.note: IT BREAKS THE IGNEOUS RULE. Described as HIGHLY POROUS, collecting rainwater 'like stony sponges'. Climbers are warned the syenite 'becomes fragile with extra humidity from rain'. An igneous rock with a real wet-weather ethic — do not assume plutonic means climbable wet.

water_features.value: Huecos — HOLD WATER FOR SEVERAL DAYS TO SEVERAL MONTHS depending on pool size and shelter

access_rules.value: Access is managed — guided and reservation systems apply on parts of the park (not independently verified in this pass)

rock.note: 'Flint-hard', glassy, and it DRIES QUICKLY — but its defining property to climbers is an 'almost complete lack of friction'. Friction-limited, and temperature/humidity matter more than hours-since-rain.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Fast — but hours-since-rain is the wrong question here; temperature and humidity dominate

rock.note: LOW-POROSITY GRANITE THAT STILL DRIES SLOWLY. Exposed sun-and-wind areas can dry in minutes; shaded rainforest boulders take a day or more in April even in good weather. Moss, seepage and shade dominate a rock with ~1% porosity.

aspect.value: Exposed sun-and-wind sectors dry in minutes; shaded rainforest sectors take a day or more. Within-crag, aspect-driven.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Much slower than its porosity predicts — biology and shade, not lithology

unmodelled_input.value: Moss and canopy drip

rock.note: VEGETATION IS THE DRYING LIMITER ON GRANITE. 'Heavily vegetated with trees growing even on boulders or granite domes,' and many climbs 'may remain wet for a day or two after a prolonged wet period'. Granite at ~1% porosity taking two days to dry is not the rock — it is canopy drip, moss and shade. IN A TEMPERATE RAINFOREST THE BIOLOGY SETS THE DRYING TIME AND THE LITHOLOGY IS NEARLY IRRELEVANT.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: A day or two after a prolonged wet period — far slower than granite predicts

unmodelled_input.value: Canopy drip, moss and shade

rock.note: Yosemite-like granite above the Skykomish.

unmodelled_input.value: A RAIN-SHADOW BOUNDARY CAN PUT TWO CRAGS AN HOUR APART IN DIFFERENT SEASONS. Being west of the Cascade crest keeps Index cool when the east side is over 90 °F.

rock.formation: Columbia River basalt, columnar, carved by the Ice Age floods
rock.note: 600+ routes, and explicitly 'one of Washington's great winter crags'. Dense columnar basalt as the wet-season option, exactly as the welding/porosity spectrum predicts.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: The regional wet-season option — dries fast enough to be the winter crag

rock.note: The NPS says plainly it is 'VERY WEAK COMPARED TO THE GRANITE AND BASALT OF MANY CLIMBING AREAS', brittle, loose on the West Side, with many old or incorrectly installed bolts. A distinct class: angular fragments in a finer matrix, so like conglomerate the MATRIX GOVERNS. No label in the RockType enum.

closure.reason: Raptor closures are typical at this park but were not verified in this pass

unmodelled_input.value: Fixed-gear condition — many old or incorrectly installed bolts

rock.note: 'Plated granite'. The plates and chickenheads ARE the holds — the same structural situation as the Needles' crystals: hold loss is a discrete feature detaching, not surface spalling.
Pocketed volcanic tuff — a third welded-tuff datapoint after Smith Rock and Penitente.

Peeling in concentric sheets like an onion as confining pressure is released. WATER GETS BEHIND EXFOLIATION SHEETS, so the drying-relevant volume is not the surface. Granite domes generally (City of Rocks, the Wichitas, Stone Mountain) share this.

unmodelled_input.value: Water behind exfoliation sheets — a volume no surface measurement sees

rock.note: HUMIDITY ALONE PRODUCES RAIN-EQUIVALENT CONDITIONS. Climbers report 'the biggest problem is heat and humidity; the effect is very similar to climbing in the rain here... slick and slippery'. Low-porosity rock, zero rainfall, unclimbable conditions — A PRECIPITATION-DRIVEN SCORE CANNOT SEE THIS AT ALL.

unmodelled_input.value: Humidity with no rainfall. One of four independent reports in the research of humidity alone deciding conditions.

rock.note: 'Very slippery and not conducive to placing solid trad gear'.

unmodelled_input.value: River level — AND UNLIKE WILLOW RIVER, A DATA SOURCE EXISTS: NOAA publishes Potomac gauges (water.noaa.gov). The only crag in the research whose unmodelled input has a named public feed.

rock.formation: Diabase sill — feldspar plus augite, salt-and-pepper, ~500 ft above the Hudson
rock.note: Dense intrusive: 0.1-0.5% porosity.
Hard and high quality.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: 'Can take a while to dry after a storm'

rock.note: Hard and high quality.

shelter.value: 'The large overhanging roofs at Foster's keep some routes dry even in the pouring rain.' GEOMETRY BEATS ROCK TYPE.

access_rules.value: An unusually explicit community ethic: 'Never climb on wet sandstone — it damages the rock permanently by pulling off crystals... If it rained in the last 24 to 48 hours, stick to the gym. THIS IS NOT A SUGGESTION.'

dries_fast_relative_to.value: 24-48h community rule

rock.note: Glacially polished, ~1000 ft, plagioclase-dominated plutonic rock with gneiss interfingering and an unusual chert-like rock welded into it. Behaves as dense plutonic rock for drying; glacial polish makes it friction-limited on the slabs.

closure.reason: Peregrine falcon closures are typical in the Adirondacks but were not verified in this pass

crags.name: Looking Glass Rock

rock.formation: Whiteside granite, ~390 Ma — an exfoliating dome
rock.note: THE HOLDS ARE MADE OF SEEPAGE. Its famous 'eyebrows' are 'thousands of horizontal wrinkles in the granite veneer, WEATHERED BY WATER SEEPING INTO THE METAMORPHOSED FELDSPAR AND MICA'. The feature climbers pull on is the record of where water runs.

water_features.value: eyebrows — a fossil seep by EROSION, where a tufa is a fossil seep by DEPOSITION

unmodelled_input.value: Verglas after freezing rain — the crag is named for it, and its whole surface is a thin exfoliating veneer

crags._why_this_crag_matters: GENERALISES THE TUFA RULE AND IS THE MOST PORTABLE FINDING IN THE RESEARCH. 'Where the holds were made by water, water still goes there.' It turns an unanswerable question — is this crag seepage-prone? — into an OBSERVABLE one a guidebook photo answers. The uncomfortable corollary: a heavily featured wall is more likely to seep than a blank one, and the features climbers travel for are the evidence.

rock.note: The other Carolina granite; Looking Glass's exfoliation is the shared mechanism.

rock.formation: Silurian dolomite — a 700 km UNESCO escarpment of limestone and dolostone

shelter.value: 'Undercut in most places, with access normally from above by rappel to a hanging belay at the lip of the overhang' — RAIN-SHELTERED BY GEOMETRY.

approach_hazard.value: Rappel access to a hanging belay

unmodelled_input.value: A sheltered, UNWASHED carbonate crag near a large water body is the pattern that concentrates chloride on fixed gear — though fresh water is not sea spray and the risk is not the same. The shelter rule inverts here: shelter from rain means no rinsing.

rock.note: Up to 300 ft out of Mazinaw Lake.

approach_hazard.value: THE APPROACH IS A BOAT — some climbs start out of the lake, so you canoe in. Lake state governs access.

unmodelled_input.value: Lake state

crags.name: Frankenjura

rock.formation: Limestone below, magnesium-enriched dolomite above; laminated lime structures in the lower layers

shelter.value: DRY ROCK CAN BE FOUND IN ALMOST ANY WEATHER, and there is a known list of crags that stay dry through long rainy spells and 'almost never get wet'. crags._tufa_rule_note: THE ONLY CLEAN CONTROL in the seven-area test: Mediterranean, same region and climate as tufa-rich Rodellar, tufas called an anomaly, no seepage reputation. The whole between-crag case for the tufa rule rests on this one crag — which is why §4.16 went looking for a within-crag control and found Rifle. seepage_prone stays null: absence of tufa proves nothing.

rock.note: 5,000+ routes on high-quality limestone north of Lake Garda, climbable most of the year and the standard fallback when the Dolomites are wet.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: The regional dry-weather fallback when the Dolomites are wet

crags.name: Rocklands

rock.note: THE DISSENTING LOCAL NORM WAS RIGHT AND THE REASON IS THE ROCK. Climbers here commonly climb after rain, 'which is definitely not the case at sandstone climbing areas in the U.S.' Table Mountain Sandstone was compressed and PARTIALLY METAMORPHOSED INTO VERY HARD QUARTZITIC SANDSTONE — it belongs with the arenites (~0% measured strength loss when wet), not the eolian class the US 24-48h rules were written for.

dries_fast_relative_to.value: Tolerates climbing after rain, unlike US eolian sandstone

crags._why_this_crag_matters: The general lesson the research keeps returning to: 'SANDSTONE' IS NOT A WET-WEATHER CLASS, and exporting a waiting period across formations is how a correct rule becomes a wrong one.

rock.note: Fragile, and more so after rain. The softness drives a glue-in bolting norm.

rock.note: VERY SOFT, weather-sculptured, and PRONE TO POLISHING QUICKLY. The polish mechanism at its most extreme — calcite at Mohs 3 under traffic.

unmodelled_input.value: THE CONDITIONS RULE IS NOT ABOUT DRYING. Afternoon thunderstorms and heat make early starts essential to avoid thunderstorms and slick rock. The limiting variables are convective-storm TIMING and humidity — a TIME-OF-DAY answer, which a daily score cannot express.

rock.note: Granite slabs at ~1,600 m.

season_gate.value: Season July to mid-October; cold from mid-October to May. AUTUMN IS MARKEDLY DRIER THAN SPRING. Altitude gates the season.

rock.note: RAIN IS OFTEN NOT THE BINDING CONSTRAINT — CONDENSATION IS. Warm moisture-laden air meeting cooler rock puts water on a wall that has seen no rain for a week. A drying model driven only by precipitation will report these crags dry and be wrong.

season_gate.value: Peak season December-February when humidity is lowest; monsoon roughly June-September leaves routes SEEPING FOR DAYS

unmodelled_input.value: IN LA NIÑA CONDITIONS CONDENSATION SEEPS OUT OF TUFA STREAKS EVEN WHEN IT IS NOT RAINING, and standard chalk turns to sludge in the humidity. That single sentence fuses three threads: condensation-as-liquid-water, tufa-as-fossil-seep, and hygroscopic chalk. Fourth independent report of humidity alone deciding conditions.

rock.note: Heavily tufa'd. THE STRONGEST CONFIRMATION OF THE TUFA RULE IN THE RESEARCH, and it states the mechanism outright: 'Even caves get wet as the rain seeps into the mountain (THIS IS HOW MOST OF THE EPIC TUFA FORM), and it can get so intense it's like it's raining in the cave interior.' The tufas are named as the PRODUCT of the seepage, by climbers, without prompting.

shelter.value: SHELTER FROM THE SKY IS NOT SHELTER FROM THE WATER HERE. It is the caves — the sheltered places — that rain inside, because the water is coming through the roof. The shelter rule inverts at a karst crag.

season_gate.value: September-December with November best; the April-September monsoon is out

approach_hazard.value: 'In wetter years most of the intermittent watercourses are still flowing, meaning that WADING WAS REQUIRED to access several of the crags.' For a meaningful minority of crags the thing rain closes is the APPROACH, not the rock.

season_gate.value: 911 mm annual; September wettest at 266 mm, January driest at 25 mm; season late October to March. Named for a waterfall 'that you only see in raining season' — the tufa-forming water is seasonal and the season is deliberately climbed around.

crags._why_this_crag_matters: DECOUPLES THE SHELTER RULE FROM THE TUFA RULE. Tufa says THIS FACE HAS HAD WATER ON IT; overhang says TODAY'S RAIN IS NOT THAT WATER. Both are true here and they are orthogonal. A model reading tufa as 'seepage-prone, suppress' would be wrong at La Boca for five months a year; a model reading overhang as 'always dry' would be wrong in September. THE ROCK-TYPE CONSTANT CANNOT RESOLVE EITHER — only a per-crag flag with a season on it can.

rock.note: The 'a bit greasy' case: a wall whose bulk is bone dry can still be greasy on a humid morning, because the SURFACE equilibrates with the air almost immediately. That is a FRICTION failure on rock that is genuinely dry — which is why a single drying output cannot serve.

unmodelled_input.value: Atmospheric humidity acting on the surface alone — sorption, not wetting
